clinical_category: Liver transplant evaluation - psychosocial and caregiver assessment
blueprint_topic: Multidisciplinary transplant evaluation, client education, and barrier mitigation
stem: During liver-transplant evaluation, a client asks, "Why does the team need to discuss my mental health, medication adherence, and caregiver plan in addition to my medical tests?" Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: These areas are assessed to identify barriers that could affect transplant success and to develop supports or treatment plans when problems can be addressed.
options.B: Any history of a mental health disorder automatically excludes a client from liver transplantation, regardless of treatment or stability.
options.C: The caregiver interview is used mainly to judge the client's social worth and is not related to practical post-transplant care needs.
options.D: Psychosocial assessment is optional because transplant candidacy is determined only by laboratory values and imaging results.

rationale: A is correct. The current AASLD/AST adult liver-transplant candidate-evaluation guideline includes a dedicated psychosocial evaluation. It recommends assessing adherence to medical directives and mental-health stability, evaluating whether adequate caregiver/social support is available for the wait-list and postoperative period, and helping identify strategies to mitigate social and financial barriers when they are found. The guideline explains that the purpose of psychosocial assessment is to identify areas requiring intervention and to support successful transplantation, not simply to exclude candidates. B is incorrect because the guideline states that even serious mental-health disorders are not absolute contraindications when appropriate treatment, stability, and support can be achieved. C is incorrect because caregiver assessment focuses on practical assistance such as transportation, medication management, and postoperative support and should not be used as a proxy for social worth. D is incorrect because liver-transplant evaluation is explicitly multidisciplinary and includes psychosocial as well as medical assessment. The final item teaches the purpose of psychosocial evaluation without stigmatizing mental illness or presenting social support as an automatic binary eligibility rule.
educational_objective: Explain that psychosocial and caregiver assessment is a core part of liver-transplant evaluation used to identify modifiable barriers, assess adherence and support needs, and develop interventions that promote safe wait-list and post-transplant care.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) and American Society of Transplantation (AST)
source_document_title: AASLD AST Practice Guideline on Adult Liver Transplantation: Candidate Evaluation
source_locator: Section 'The Psychosocial Evaluation' → Question 16 and Guideline Statements 35-42: assessment of adherence, mental-health stability, caregiver/social support, and mitigation of social/financial barriers. 'Rationale and Background' under the same section: goal is to identify psychosocial areas requiring intervention; relevant domains include adherence, caregiver support, cognitive capacity, psychiatric/substance-use issues, illness understanding, coping, and treatment understanding. Later Psychosocial guidance: mental-health disorders are not absolute contraindications when treated/stabilized and adequate support is available.
source_claim_supported: The current AASLD/AST guideline directly supports comprehensive psychosocial evaluation of adherence, mental health, caregiver/social support, and modifiable barriers as part of liver-transplant candidate assessment and explicitly rejects automatic exclusion based on mental-health diagnosis alone.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment → Management of Care, printed p. 7 (PDF p. 10): identify/collaborate with multidisciplinary team members and assess need for referrals/orders. Appendix A → Management of Care → Collaboration with Multidisciplinary Team, printed p. 21 (PDF p. 24): identify significant information to report to other disciplines and review plan of care for continuity; Concepts of Management: coordinate/manage care and act as liaison between client and others.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's broad 'comprehensive evaluation' recall question into a client-teaching and care-coordination scenario grounded in the 2026 AASLD/AST candidate-evaluation guideline. The final item explains why psychosocial, adherence, and caregiver domains are assessed, removes stigmatizing or absolute exclusion assumptions, and maps directly to NCSBN Management of Care multidisciplinary coordination.
audit_findings: The source item was directionally correct but too generic and used an imprecise UNOS/AASLD citation without an exact locator.
Fresh review of the current 2026 AASLD/AST candidate-evaluation guideline directly supports psychosocial assessment of adherence, mental health, caregiver support, and modifiable barriers.

The final item avoids a common harmful overstatement: a mental-health diagnosis or imperfect social support does not automatically exclude a candidate; the transplant team should evaluate and mitigate barriers where possible.
Distractors test automatic psychiatric exclusion, social-worth judgment, and medical-only evaluation; none is defensible under the current guideline.
